Ridge regression

Scaling of predictors

The lasso and variable selection

Choosing $\lambda$ by cross-validation

The "loss + penalty" framework

::: notes - Based on ISLR Section 6.2. We implement ridge in closed form and the lasso by coordinate descent so that glmnet is no longer a black box. ::: ## Shrinkage Methods: Ridge Regression and Lasso - Subset selection fits least squares on a *subset* of the predictors. - Alternative: fit a model with **all** $p$ predictors using a technique that *constrains* or *regularizes* the coefficients, i.e., **shrinks** them toward zero. - Shrinking the coefficient estimates can significantly reduce their variance. Recall least squares minimizes $$ \text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p\beta_jx_{ij}\Big)^2. $$ ## Ridge Regression $$ \hat\bbeta^R_\lambda = \argmin_{\bbeta}\;\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p\beta_jx_{ij}\Big)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2 = \text{RSS} + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2 $$ - $\lambda\ge0$ is a **tuning parameter**; $\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2$ is the **shrinkage penalty** (the intercept is not penalized). - $\lambda = 0$: least squares. $\lambda\to\infty$: all $\beta_j\to 0$. - Closed form (centered $\by$, standardized $\bX$): $$ \hat\bbeta^R_\lambda = (\bX^\T\bX + \lambda\bI)^{-1}\bX^\T\by $$ ::: fact $\bX^\T\bX + \lambda\bI$ is invertible for every $\lambda > 0$, even when $p > n$ or the predictors are collinear. ::: ## Ridge from Scratch: Credit Data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ISLR2) y <- Credit$Balance X <- model.matrix(Balance ~ ., data = Credit)[, -1] n <- nrow(X) Xs <- scale(X) * sqrt(n / (n - 1)) # standardize with divisor n yc <- y - mean(y) ridge <- function(lambda) solve(crossprod(Xs) + lambda * diag(ncol(Xs)), crossprod(Xs, yc)) lambdas <- 10^seq(-2, 5, length = 100) B <- sapply(lambdas, ridge) rownames(B) <- colnames(X) round(B[c("Income", "Limit", "Rating", "StudentYes"), c(1, 50, 100)], 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] Income -274.6 -193.3 0.84 Limit 438.6 269.9 1.57 Rating 177.1 262.5 1.57 StudentYes 127.7 116.2 0.47 ``` ::: ::: ## Ridge Coefficient Paths ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) hl <- c("Income", "Limit", "Rating", "StudentYes") cols <- ifelse(rownames(B) %in% hl, c("black", "red", "blue", "orange")[match(rownames(B), hl)], "gray80") matplot(lambdas, t(B), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = cols, log = "x", xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "Standardized coefficients") legend("topright", hl, col = c("black", "red", "blue", "orange"), lwd = 2, bty = "n") ratio <- apply(B, 2, function(b) sqrt(sum(b^2))) / sqrt(sum(B[, 1]^2)) matplot(ratio, t(B), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = cols, xlab = expression(paste("||", hat(beta)[lambda]^R, "||"[2], " / ||", hat(beta), "||"[2])), ylab = "") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/04-ridge-lasso/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - Left: each curve is one predictor's coefficient as a function of $\lambda$. Right: the same, indexed by $\|\hat\bbeta^R_\lambda\|_2/\|\hat\bbeta\|_2$. ## Ridge Regression: Scaling of Predictors - Least squares estimates are **scale equivariant**: multiplying $X_j$ by $c$ scales $\hat\beta_j$ by $1/c$. - Ridge estimates can change **substantially** when a predictor is rescaled, because of the penalty $\sum_j\beta_j^2$. - Therefore, standardize the predictors first: $$ \tilde x_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij}}{\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2}} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} X2 <- Xs; X2[, "Income"] <- X2[, "Income"] * 1000 # income in dollars, not $1000s r1 <- solve(crossprod(Xs) + 50 * diag(11), crossprod(Xs, yc))["Income", ] r2 <- solve(crossprod(X2) + 50 * diag(11), crossprod(X2, yc))["Income", ] * 1000 c(standardized = r1, rescaled = r2) # not the same fit! ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` standardized.Income rescaled.Income -154.3 -203.0 ``` ::: ::: ## Why Does Ridge Help? Bias-Variance Trade-off ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); ns <- 50; p <- 45; beta <- rnorm(p, sd = 0.4) Xsim <- matrix(rnorm(ns * p), ns); Xtest <- matrix(rnorm(500 * p), 500) ftest <- Xtest %*% beta lam <- 10^seq(-2, 3, length = 30) fits <- replicate(100, { ysim <- Xsim %*% beta + rnorm(ns) sapply(lam, function(l) Xtest %*% solve(crossprod(Xsim) + l * diag(p), crossprod(Xsim, ysim))) }, simplify = "array") # 500 x 30 x 100 bias2 <- colMeans((apply(fits, c(1, 2), mean) - as.vector(ftest))^2) variance <- colMeans(apply(fits, c(1, 2), var)) matplot(lam, cbind(bias2, variance, bias2 + variance), type = "l", lwd = 3, lty = 1, log = "x", col = c("black", "#2E8B57", "#C2185B"), xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "") legend("top", c("squared bias", "variance", "MSE"), col = c("black", "#2E8B57", "#C2185B"), lwd = 3, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/04-ridge-lasso/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: notes - With p = 45 close to n = 50, least squares has huge variance. Ridge trades a little bias for a large reduction in variance. ::: ## The Lasso - Ridge always includes **all** $p$ predictors in the final model; it cannot select variables. - The **lasso** minimizes $$ \sum_{i=1}^n\Big(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^p\beta_jx_{ij}\Big)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^p|\beta_j| = \text{RSS} + \lambda\|\bbeta\|_1 $$ - The $\ell_1$ penalty forces some coefficients to be **exactly zero** when $\lambda$ is large enough $\Rightarrow$ **variable selection**, **sparse** models. - As with ridge, choosing $\lambda$ is critical: cross-validation. ## Lasso by Coordinate Descent Minimizing over one coordinate $\beta_j$ with the others fixed has a closed-form **soft-thresholding** solution $$ \beta_j \leftarrow \frac{S\!\left(\sum_i x_{ij}r_{ij},\ \lambda/2\right)}{\sum_i x_{ij}^2},\qquad S(z,\gamma) = \text{sign}(z)(|z|-\gamma)_+ , $$ where $r_{ij} = y_i - \sum_{k\neq j}x_{ik}\beta_k$ is the partial residual. Cycle over $j$ until convergence. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} soft <- function(z, g) sign(z) * pmax(abs(z) - g, 0) lasso_cd <- function(X, y, lambda, beta = rep(0, ncol(X)), tol = 1e-4, maxit = 1e4) { r <- as.vector(y - X %*% beta); xx <- colSums(X^2) for (it in 1:maxit) { old <- beta for (j in seq_along(beta)) { r <- r + X[, j] * beta[j] # partial residual beta[j] <- soft(sum(X[, j] * r), lambda / 2) / xx[j] r <- r - X[, j] * beta[j] } if (max(abs(beta - old)) < tol) break } beta } ``` ::: ## Lasso Coefficient Paths: Credit Data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lamL <- 10^seq(5, 0, length = 80); b <- rep(0, ncol(Xs)); BL <- matrix(NA, ncol(Xs), length(lamL)) for (k in seq_along(lamL)) BL[, k] <- b <- lasso_cd(Xs, yc, lamL[k], beta = b) # warm starts rownames(BL) <- colnames(X) matplot(lamL, t(BL), type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = cols, log = "x", xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "Standardized coefficients") legend("topright", hl, col = c("black", "red", "blue", "orange"), lwd = 2, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/04-ridge-lasso/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} apply(BL[, c(20, 40, 60)], 2, function(b) names(which(b != 0))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [[1]] [1] "Income" "Limit" "Rating" "Cards" "Age" [6] "StudentYes" [[2]] [1] "Income" "Limit" "Rating" "Cards" "Age" [6] "Education" "OwnYes" "StudentYes" "MarriedYes" "RegionSouth" [11] "RegionWest" [[3]] [1] "Income" "Limit" "Rating" "Cards" "Age" [6] "Education" "OwnYes" "StudentYes" "MarriedYes" "RegionSouth" [11] "RegionWest" ``` ::: ::: ## Comparison with `glmnet` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(glmnet) # glmnet minimizes RSS/(2n) + lambda * penalty, so lambda_glmnet = lambda / (2n) g <- glmnet(Xs, yc, alpha = 1, lambda = 1000 / (2 * nrow(Xs)), standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE, thresh = 1e-14) cbind(ours = lasso_cd(Xs, yc, 1000, tol = 1e-10, maxit = 1e6), glmnet = as.numeric(coef(g))[-1]) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ours glmnet [1,] -268.884 -268.884 [2,] 427.071 427.082 [3,] 182.638 182.627 [4,] 22.932 22.932 [5,] -9.839 -9.839 [6,] -2.159 -2.159 [7,] -3.863 -3.863 [8,] 126.237 126.238 [9,] -2.806 -2.805 [10,] 2.018 2.018 [11,] 4.173 4.173 ``` ::: ::: ## Choosing $\lambda$ by Cross-Validation ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(Xs))); lamCV <- 10^seq(4, 0, length = 20) cv_err <- rowMeans(sapply(1:5, function(k) { tr <- folds != k; mx <- colMeans(Xs[tr, ]); my <- mean(yc[tr]) Xtr <- sweep(Xs[tr, ], 2, mx); Xte <- sweep(Xs[!tr, ], 2, mx); b <- rep(0, ncol(Xs)) sapply(lamCV, function(l) { # warm starts along the path b <<- lasso_cd(Xtr, yc[tr] - my, l, beta = b) mean((yc[!tr] - my - Xte %*% b)^2) }) })) plot(lamCV, cv_err, log = "x", type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#003366", xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "5-fold CV error") abline(v = lamCV[which.min(cv_err)], lty = 2, col = "red") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/04-ridge-lasso/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: tip In practice: `cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)` does this (with the "one-standard-error" rule as an option). We study cross-validation in Chapter 8. ::: ## The Variable Selection Property of the Lasso Why does the lasso, unlike ridge, give coefficients that are **exactly** zero? Equivalent constrained problems: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Lasso:** $\displaystyle\min_{\bbeta}\ \text{RSS}\quad\text{s.t.}\ \sum_{j=1}^p|\beta_j|\le s$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Ridge:** $\displaystyle\min_{\bbeta}\ \text{RSS}\quad\text{s.t.}\ \sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2\le s$ ::: :::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/04-ridge-lasso/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: The RSS ellipses first touch the $\ell_1$ diamond at a **corner** (some $\beta_j = 0$); the $\ell_2$ disk has no corners. ## Flexibility of the "Loss + Penalty" Framework $$ \text{Minimize}\ \ \color{blue}{\text{Loss}} + \lambda\,\color{red}{\text{Penalty}} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Loss |Penalty |Algorithm | |:-----------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------| |Hinge: $\sum_i[1-y_if(\mathbf x_i)]_+$ |$\lambda\|\mathbf w\|_2^2$ |SVM | |Squared error: $\sum_i(y_i - f(\mathbf x_i))^2$ |$\lambda\|\mathbf w\|_2^2$ |Ridge regression | |Squared error |$\lambda\|\mathbf w\|_1$ |Lasso | |Squared error |$\lambda_1\|\mathbf w\|_1 + \lambda_2\|\mathbf w\|_2^2$ |Elastic net | |Hinge |$\lambda\|\mathbf w\|_1$ |1-norm SVM | |Negative log-likelihood |$\lambda\|\mathbf w\|_1$ |Penalized logistic regression | ::: ::: ## Summary ::: instructions - Ridge: $\ell_2$ penalty, closed form $(\bX^\T\bX+\lambda\bI)^{-1}\bX^\T\by$, shrinks but keeps all predictors. - Lasso: $\ell_1$ penalty, soft-thresholding by coordinate descent, produces sparse models. - Standardize predictors before penalizing. - Tune $\lambda$ by cross-validation; penalization trades bias for variance. ::: ::: your-turn Modify `lasso_cd()` to fit the **elastic net** $\text{RSS} + \lambda[\alpha\|\bbeta\|_1 + (1-\alpha)\|\bbeta\|_2^2]$. (Hint: the update becomes $S(\cdot)/(1 + \cdots)$.) :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
